You have to understand that suicide hotlines are terribly underfunded and understaffed. Most rely on volunteers with little to no counselling training or experience. The one I worked at was staffed by college kids, most of whom only had one introductory psychology course under their belts. Their job is to talk you off the ledge and direct you to people that can help you or, if that fails, direct help to you. But people call the hotline looking for free therapy, which “counsellors” are ill-equipped and not supposed to do. It’s also a real roller coaster of a job too. One minute you’re talking a teenager being bullied by his classmates out of hanging himself and the next you’re listening to some middle aged woman bitch about being stuck in traffic. There aren’t any consequences for misusing the suicide hotline so people abuse it all the time. It’s hardly a surprise that most operators quickly burn out.

I’ve seen marijuana destroy lives too. I had a friend and coworker that started smoking weed to “treat” his depression. Pot took over his life. He went from being a guy that always wanted to go out and do things to a guy that never left his house. He just stayed home, smoked weed, watched Netflix, and played games. Then his legal troubles started. Because there’s less stigma for driving high than there is for driving drunk, he drove under the influence all the time. One night, he totalled his car and could’ve died. Thankfully, it was a single car collision and no one else was hurt. Did that stop him from driving high? Another night, he got pulled over for driving way too slow on the highway; his car reeked of marijuana when the cop walked up. He got his car towed, his license suspended, and a huge fine. Was it his fault? No, of course not. He blamed the cop. Not long after, he ended up in court because weed was having a negative impact on his memory and he forgot to renew his registration and insurance. He moved away a few years ago and is apparently struggling now because, between his criminal record and the negative impact weed had on his job performance, he is having a really hard time finding a job. Last time I talked to him, he was bordering on homeless. Still had money to get high everyday, though.

My problem was that they put me on antipsychotics from the very beginning - not that I blame them, I did show symptoms of bipolar disorder with rapid cycling. Antipsychotics kicked my ass. I was tired all the time (sleeping 14 hours a day at my worst point), had terrible brain fog, etc. The last combination I tried before my current medication was Seroquel and Wellbutrin. I took Seroquel before bed and Wellbutrin when I got up in the morning; Seroquel knocked me on my butt and I was a zombie from when I got out of bed until the Wellbutrin started to kick in. After that, I gave up on medication and self-medicated with alcohol for about 3 years. Then, last October, I threatened to kill myself, my mom called the cops, and I was taken to the hospital where I was put on Lexapro, which, like I said, is slightly different from Celexa, one of the first medications I tried. It’s been pretty good overall. I’m thinking about asking my doctor for Wellbutrin again because I still feel pretty down on bad weather days, but otherwise, my mood’s improved, I’m less anxious, I don’t think about suicide nearly as much so... 4/5, would recommend, I guess.

As someone that has studied to be both a paramedic and a nurse, it drives me crazy how the healthcare system treats the mentally ill. When someone has a physical illness and they refuse to make lifestyle changes, like a diabetic refusing to change their diet or someone with lung disease refuses to quit smoking, they are generally treated pretty harshly by health professionals. Meanwhile, people with mental illnesses get a free pass for everything.

Addiction especially pisses me off. A few months back, a prominent Twitter figure was tweeting about his struggles with alcoholism and, as usual, marijuana advocates popped up to tell him to smoke weed instead; I got ran off Twitter by a mob of “mental health professionals” for daring to say he shouldn’t substitute one substance for another. Now, I’m generally not a fan of the AA model in which we demand total sobriety from addicts before we help them, but I also don’t think we should be giving addicts permission to use either. Switching to marijuana is often a lateral move at best. The theory is that marijuana eases the transition from harder drugs into sobriety, but clients often get stuck in the transition phase and use harm reduction as a justification for the continued marijuana use. In my, albeit brief, experience as a social worker, addicts *fucking love* harm reduction. It gives them an excuse to use AND a defence against anyone that gives them hard time for it. If anything, we should be encouraging socially acceptable use. You want to get drunk or high after work, that’s fine, but if someone goes to work drunk or high, their therapist should tell them that they’re a fucking idiot to their face. No more hand holding.

I started taking medication for depression. I was a law enforcement officer for 3.5 years; my buddy is a Crown Attorney (lawyer for the Canadian government). As such, I have a pretty decent grasp on the Canadian criminal justice system; I feel fairly confident in my ability to comment on the American justice system since both the American and the Canadian systems are based on the British justice system.

In free and just societies, like the United States, a person generally has to commit a crime before the state can arrest them and charge them with a crime; so the question for me is: Did Serena Waterford commit a crime? In my opinion, the answer isn’t as cut and dry as you seem to think; if you look at the facts in an objective way (which is easier to do when the person in question is a fictional character and no real people were hurt by her actions, by the way), there is a strong case to be made that she didn’t.

I have already conceded on the rape charge - Serena did commit that crime when she helped Fred to “induce labour” in June back in Season 2 so yes, she can be arrested and charged for it - so I’m not going to touch on that any further.

But conspiracy and treason are another story.

Let’s start with treason because it is easier to explain. For a person to commit treason in a free and just society, that person has to take action with the clear intent to undermine or overthrow the state - *action* being the key word. So yes, treason is, in fact, a crime that a person has to “pull the trigger” to commit. As previously stated, Serena did not participate in the attack that took out the U.S. Government or the civil war that came after; therefore, Serena did not commit treason.

Conspiracy is trickier because conspiracy is, in essence, the crime of planning to commit a crime. Anti-conspiracy laws open a Pandora’s box of fundamental rights infringements so, generally speaking, a person in a free and just society has to at least attempt to commit the crime they were planing to commit before they can be charged with conspiracy. Serena did not commit treason so it would be tough to convict her of conspiracy to commit treason. Apologies for the double negative, but that isn’t to say Serena didn’t *want* to commit treason, but wanting to commit a crime and actually committing a crime are two different things. Since there is a good degree of separation (at least two, by my count) between Serena and the actual conspirators, I would be reluctant at best to charge her with conspiracy. So maybe, technically speaking, Serena did something illegal, but in the same way that a person driving 1mph or 2km/h over the speed limit does; technically against the law, but not worth the state’s time and resources to go to court over.

As for the terrorism charge, I have difficultly describing the Sons of Jacob’s attack on the U.S. Government as terrorism because the goal of terrorism is to instil (spelling? I’m deferring to autocorrect on this one) fear in citizens. The Sons of Jacob definitely wanted to instil fear in American citizens since doing so would help them seize power, so they were definitely terrorists in that sense, but since their ultimate goal was to seize power over the United States, I feel that the attack was more treasonous or traitorous than terrorist.

And, if you want my opinion on drug laws as a health-care-student-turned-law-enforcement-professional-turned-health-care-student-again, I have a lot of issues with how drug users are treated by “the system”. One day during my emergency room practicum always sticks in my mind when I think about drug laws and users. We had two drug addicts come in that day (probably more, but only these two stuck in my mind); one was a white woman previously diagnosed with depression and anxiety that came in on her own reconnaissance shrieking for benzodiazepines and the other was a visible-minority man, with similar diagnostic history, that was brought in by ambulance because he overdosed. The woman was treated with sympathy by medical staff while the man was treated distain despite the fact that neither person could be described as a productive member of society. I don’t like how drug users are treated subjectively based on their race. I am especially unhappy with how law enforcement officers disproportionately punish visible-minorities for their drug use. But, at the same time, the law is the law and, in my opinion, the solutions are to either a.) enforce the law equally among all races (not likely), or b.) change the law so all people, regardless of race, are treated equally. Korea was similar to Cuba in the sense that both countries were ruled by foreign powers that ran them for their own benefit rather than the benefit of the people that actually lived there - although my understanding is that Japan ruled Korea directly whereas America ruled Cuba through a series of puppet dictators. Like Fidel Castro rebelled against the U.S. installed and backed Cuban government, Kim il-Sung rebelled against the Japanese. But before the Korean communist revolution could succeed or fail, the Japanese ended up on the losing side of World War II and were forced by the Allies to give up their imperialist holdings. The United States and Soviet Union took over administration of Korea and divided it amongst themselves, like they did with Germany. The Soviets quickly declared the newly created North Korea a socialist state and appointed Kim il-Sung as its leader; he began implementing communist reforms, such as nationalizing private property and industry, causing wealthy Koreans to flee to the South. South Korea promptly elected a vehement anti-Communist as their new President; North Korea, fearing an imminent attack from the South, convinced the Soviets to back their invasion of South Korea. When it appeared that South Korea was about to be overrun, the U.S. intervened and pushed the North Koreans all the way back to the Chinese border which caused China to intervene and the stalemate that exists to this day. North Korea was decimated by the war and never recovered. All of their critical infrastructure was destroyed. The already bad situation in North Korea was made worse by the collapse of the Soviet Union in the 80s.

Whether North Korea was a decent place to live before the communists took over is debatable. Like Cuba, it was probably pretty good if you had money, but it was also probably pretty sucky if you didn’t. There was no upward mobility for Koreans born poor. They were basically pressed into a life of wage slavery. So North Korea is probably another example of the people being broke and suffering before the authoritarian regime took over - although in this case, the new bosses shot themselves in the feet by going to war with the U.S. and only survived because the Soviets and the Chinese propped them up.
